exhibits.title: Homo sapiens
exhibits.change: Our own species appears — across Africa, not in a single garden.
exhibits.context: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to about 315,000 years ago, have modern-looking faces with more elongated braincases. Together with remains from Omo Kibish and Florisbad, they suggest Homo sapiens emerged across a network of African populations, with the fully modern skull shape settling in later.
exhibits.significance: Everything else in this Museum from here onward was made by this species.

uncertainty.note: Whether modern humans arose in one region or through gene flow among many African populations ('African multiregionalism') is debated.

sources.note: Hublin et al. 2017; Richter et al. 2017, Nature.

exhibits.title: Red Ochre

when.display: regular use from c. 300,000 years ago

exhibits.change: People began collecting and grinding red earth — colour for its own sake, or for meaning.
exhibits.context: Ground and scraped pieces of iron-rich ochre become common in African Middle Stone Age sites. Ochre can be used as an adhesive ingredient, a sunscreen or a hide treatment, but its selection for bright reds suggests display as well.
exhibits.significance: Colour is one of the earliest possible signs of symbolic behaviour.

uncertainty.note: Functional versus symbolic uses of early ochre are hard to separate.

exhibits.title: Complex Language

when.display: no direct trace — estimates range widely, likely by 100,000 years ago

regions.note: Most likely among early Homo sapiens in Africa; whether Neanderthals had comparable language is debated.

exhibits.change: Thoughts could be shared, stacked and passed on — knowledge began to accumulate.
exhibits.context: Speech leaves no fossils. Researchers infer it from anatomy, genetics, the complexity of tools, and symbolic objects such as beads and engravings. Estimates for when fully modern language appeared range from more than 300,000 years ago to about 100,000 years ago.
exhibits.significance: Language made cumulative culture possible: each generation could start from where the last one stopped. It is the engine behind every other exhibit here.

uncertainty.note: There is no consensus on when, how gradually, or in which species complex language arose.

exhibits.title: The First Synthetic Material

regions.note: Compound ochre-and-gum adhesives, c. 70,000 years ago.

exhibits.change: Heating birch bark produced a glue that does not exist in nature.
exhibits.context: Birch tar requires heating bark with limited oxygen. Tar-coated flakes from Campitello, Italy, are about 200,000 years old, and Neanderthals later made it at Königsaue. Modern humans in southern Africa independently mixed ochre and plant gums into strong adhesives.
exhibits.significance: Transforming a material by controlled heat is the conceptual ancestor of ceramics, metallurgy and chemistry.

sources.note: Mazza et al. 2006; Wadley et al. 2009, PNAS (Sibudu).

exhibits.title: Denisovans
exhibits.change: A human population first recognised from DNA in a finger bone.
exhibits.context: In 2010, genome sequencing of a tiny bone from Denisova Cave revealed a previously unknown group related to Neanderthals. A jaw from the Tibetan Plateau shows they lived at high altitude, and their DNA survives in people of Oceania and Asia today.
exhibits.significance: A human group identified from genetics before its skeleton was well known — a new way of reading the past.

uncertainty.note: Their appearance, range and relationship to fossils such as Homo longi are still being worked out.

sources.note: Krause et al. 2010; Reich et al. 2010, Nature.

exhibits.title: Shell Beads
exhibits.change: Pierced shells strung to be worn — objects that say who you are.
exhibits.context: Perforated Nassarius and Tritia shells, often ochre-stained and worn smooth by string, appear in North Africa by about 142,000 years ago and later in the Levant and southern Africa.
exhibits.significance: Personal ornaments imply social identity and shared meanings — a strong marker of symbolic thought.

exhibits.title: Deliberate Burial

site.label: Panga ya Saidi, Kenya (c. 78,000 years ago)

regions.note: Neanderthal burials such as La Chapelle-aux-Saints.

exhibits.change: The dead were laid in dug graves, sometimes with ochre or objects.
exhibits.context: Burials at Qafzeh and Skhul, and a child's grave at Panga ya Saidi in Kenya about 78,000 years ago, show deliberate placement of bodies. Neanderthals also buried some of their dead.
exhibits.significance: Care for the dead suggests abstract ideas about people, loss and perhaps an afterlife.

uncertainty.note: Claims of much older burial (e.g. Homo naledi, c. 250,000 years ago) are strongly contested.

sources.note: Martinón-Torres et al. 2021, Nature (Panga ya Saidi).

exhibits.title: A Paint Workshop
exhibits.change: Abalone shells used as containers for a mixed, ochre-rich paint.
exhibits.context: Two toolkits in Blombos Cave held ground ochre, bone marrow fat, charcoal and grindstones inside abalone shells — a recipe prepared in stages (reported 2011).
exhibits.significance: The oldest known 'recipe': mixing ingredients in a container to make a new substance.

exhibits.title: The Blombos Engravings
exhibits.change: Crosshatched lines deliberately scratched and drawn on ochre and stone.
exhibits.context: Pieces of ochre engraved with crosshatched patterns, and a silcrete flake with lines drawn in ochre crayon (reported 2018), are among the oldest known abstract designs.
exhibits.significance: Deliberate, repeated patterns: marks meant to be seen.

uncertainty.note: Whether the patterns carried meaning or were decorative cannot be known.

exhibits.title: Katanda Harpoons
exhibits.change: Barbed bone points for spearing large river fish.
exhibits.context: Barbed bone harpoon points were found with catfish remains along the Semliki River and dated to around 90,000 years ago, far older than similar tools elsewhere.
exhibits.significance: Sophisticated bone technology and aquatic foods in the Middle Stone Age of central Africa.

uncertainty.note: The early dating was controversial when published and remains discussed.

sources.note: Yellen et al. 1995; Brooks et al. 1995, Science.

exhibits.title: Heat-Treated Stone
exhibits.change: Heating stone before knapping made it flake more cleanly.
exhibits.context: Silcrete at Pinnacle Point shows the lustre and structure of controlled heating. Getting the temperature and timing right is a multi-step process learned and passed on.
exhibits.significance: Deliberately changing a material's properties with fire — pyrotechnology — long before pottery or metal.

exhibits.title: The Great Dispersal
exhibits.change: Modern humans spread from Africa across Asia to Australia, then Europe.
exhibits.context: Genetics shows that most people living outside Africa descend from populations that left roughly 70,000–50,000 years ago. Earlier forays reached the Levant and Arabia but left fewer traces in living people.
exhibits.significance: Within a few tens of thousands of years one species occupied every habitable continent except the Americas.

uncertainty.note: Routes, timing and the number of dispersals are still debated; some fossils (e.g. Misliya, Apidima) suggest earlier exits.

exhibits.title: Crossing to Sahul
exhibits.change: People crossed open sea, out of sight of land, and reached Australia.
exhibits.context: Even at the lowest Ice Age sea levels, reaching Sahul (Australia and New Guinea) required crossings of tens of kilometres through Wallacea. Madjedbebe has been dated to about 65,000 years ago; other researchers favour about 50,000–47,000.
exhibits.significance: The oldest clear evidence of purposeful sea voyaging — by watercraft that have not survived.

uncertainty.note: The 65,000-year date at Madjedbebe is contested.

sources.note: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature; O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS.

exhibits.title: Bow and Arrow
exhibits.change: Stored energy in a bent stave launched a small point with lethal speed.
exhibits.context: Tiny stone points from Sibudu carry impact damage and residues consistent with arrows about 64,000 years ago. Grotte Mandrin in France has the oldest proposed arrowheads in Europe, about 54,000 years ago.
exhibits.significance: Hunting at a distance, with less risk, using a mechanical device that stores energy — the first of its kind.

uncertainty.note: Bows rarely survive; the evidence is indirect (points, damage, residues).

sources.note: Lombard & Phillipson 2010, Antiquity; Metz et al. 2023, Science Advances.

exhibits.title: Red Marks in Iberian Caves

site.label: La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales, Spain

exhibits.change: Uranium–thorium dates suggest Neanderthals painted lines and hand stencils.
exhibits.context: Dating of mineral crusts over red markings in three Spanish caves, published in 2018, gave minimum ages before modern humans reached Europe — implying Neanderthal authors.
exhibits.significance: If confirmed, symbolic image-making was not unique to our species.

uncertainty.note: The dating method and sampling have been challenged.

exhibits.title: Shared Ancestry

when.display: main Neanderthal admixture c. 60,000–45,000 years ago (genetic estimate)

regions.note: Denisovan ancestry is highest in Oceania.

exhibits.change: Modern humans met Neanderthals and Denisovans — and had children together.
exhibits.context: Most people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA; many people in Oceania also carry Denisovan DNA. Some inherited variants affect immunity and adaptation to high altitude.
exhibits.significance: Human history is a braided river, not a single line — and that braid is written in living genomes.
